projects.name: Decoding gestures across days
projects.summary: Can a decoder recognize the same attempted movement as neural recordings change from one session to the next?
paragraphs: Approach

I developed CoDCR, a supervised contrastive decoder that brings recordings of the same gesture closer together across sessions while separating different gestures. I evaluated it on intracortical recordings from one BrainGate participant with tetraplegia across three tasks with 10–48 gesture classes.
Across-session performance

CoDCR achieved the highest mean trial-level macro-F1 on all three tasks, both with and without labeled calibration. Overall macro-F1 was 78.78%, 8.19 percentage points above NoMAD, the strongest baseline. Compared with raw features, CEBRA, and a GRU, the learned representations showed lower relative centroid drift and tighter within-class grouping relative to the distance between classes.
Calibration

On a ten-class finger task, pretraining followed by calibration with 150 labeled trials (about five minutes) achieved 85.77% macro-F1. Training from scratch with 530 labeled trials achieved 80.20%. These comparisons describe offline decoding for this participant.

projects.name: Aligning finger movements 13 months apart
projects.summary: We used flow matching to align motor cortical recordings from two sessions covering the same 31 individuated finger gestures.
paragraphs: Recordings

The two sessions from one BrainGate2 participant were separated by 13 months and shared 541 neural features. We learned a continuous nonlinear velocity field that transported neural activity from one session into the representation space of the other.
Evaluation

Nearest-centroid classification of trial-averaged activity reached 98.4% after transport into the reference session and 97.7% in the reverse direction. I evaluated the alignment against CCA and linear interpolation and examined gesture-specific velocity coherence and within- versus between-class distances.

projects.name: Neural activity before approach–avoidance decisions
projects.summary: In 30 participants, I tested when intracranial recordings could predict an upcoming approach–avoidance choice.
paragraphs: Analysis

In Todd Herrington’s group, I built a within-participant pipeline for stereo-EEG (sEEG) spectral power. I compared time-averaged, time-resolved, and temporal-generalization analyses. Linear classifiers, tree ensembles, CNNs, and GRUs were evaluated on matched trial-level splits.
Timing and validation

Activity in the second before the response predicted the upcoming choice above chance (cluster-corrected p = .0099). Feature selection and preprocessing used training data only. I also examined regional and frequency contributions using ablation, held-out permutation importance, and participant-level analyses.

projects.name: Decoding movement through dynamics
projects.summary: I studied whether a neural decoder could predict a small set of movement controls and use them to generate smooth trajectories.
paragraphs: Model

I combined a convolutional Transformer with a state-space dynamic movement primitive (SS-DMP). The encoder inferred movement controls from neural history. A subject-specific prior was estimated from training kinematics.
Benchmarks

On ECoG and multi-session spiking benchmarks, the model achieved best or tied-best decoding accuracy and produced smoother trajectories. R² was 0.44 on M2 (RMSE 0.70, MSJ 1.62) and 0.42 on MouseTrack (RMSE 0.72). Performance degraded more slowly on chronologically held-out sessions than for the Transformer, LSTM, and Kalman baselines.

projects.name: What does motor cortex add beyond task geometry?
projects.summary: I measured how much neural signals add to finger-velocity predictions once the target, starting position, and elapsed time are known.
paragraphs: Finger velocity

Across 38 LINK sessions in one macaque, adding motor cortical spiking-band power improved held-out predictions in every session. Including the preceding 100 ms of measured finger position reduced the gain in every session. Across 20 prespecified confirmation sessions, the mean reduction in squared prediction error fell from 4.63% to 2.05%.
Trial pairing and reaching

Replacing neural residuals with residuals from matched trials increased error in all 20 confirmation sessions. In a separate continuous-reaching analysis involving two other macaques, recent cursor position also reduced the benefit of neural input in the prespecified linear models.

projects.name: State-space decoding of hand movements
projects.summary: I modeled movement phase and finger trajectories from epidural ECoG using a hidden Markov model and state-specific dynamical systems.
paragraphs: Decoder

I modeled four motor phases (rest, flexion, hold, and extension) and used the estimated phase probabilities to combine linear dynamical systems for trajectory prediction across six gestures. Mean squared error was 0.068, compared with 0.167 for the RNN baseline.
Related work
I also developed a cross-modal framework for wrist movement and ECoG, using a recurrent encoder and contrastive learning to align neural and kinematic representations.

projects.name: NeuroScribe: generating trajectories from EEG
projects.summary: NeuroScribe couples an EEG encoder to a movement-primitive decoder that predicts the parameters of a trajectory.
paragraphs: Approach and results

I trained the STFEnc encoder and an Auto-DMP decoder to estimate basis-function weights, goals, and scaling factors. NeuroScribe achieved the lowest mean squared error among the compared methods on SMR-BCI (3.42) and SignEEG v1.0 (9.24), with mean squared jerk of 0.82 and 1.95, respectively.

projects.name: Learning spatial and spectral features from EEG
projects.summary: STFEnc combines graph convolutions and connectome-informed priors with temporal and spectral features.
paragraphs: Evaluation
I preprocessed EEG recordings using MNE-Python and developed the encoder in PyTorch. Across the evaluated data, STFEnc achieved 80.78% average accuracy, compared with 74.24% for EEGNet.
